Dear Jyoti Dadi,
I've been thinking about Sunday since I got back to the hostel. When you said, "I wish I had fought to finish Class 10 instead of keeping quiet," you laughed afterwards, but your voice didn't.
I want you to know I didn't hear it as "now you must top everything for me." I heard it as a map. You showed me which silence cost you.
So here's what I did this week. I put my name down for the English debate, which terrifies me. I haven't asked Professor Rao about the research project yet, but I will by Friday. Some risks aren't worth it, like skipping sleep for marks. These ones feel like they'll let me sleep well at sixty.
Your granddaughter who talks too much,
Ankita

qa.q: What did Jyoti Dadi say she wished on Sunday?
qa.a: That she had fought to finish Class 10 instead of keeping quiet.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel hearing Dadi's regret?
qa.a: She was moved and thoughtful, noticing Dadi's voice didn't laugh, and chose to treat the regret as a map rather than a weight on her.

qa.q: Which risks does Ankita choose, and why does she skip others?
qa.a: She signs up for the English debate and plans to ask Professor Rao about the project, but won't skip sleep for marks, because only some risks will give her future self peace.

qa.q: How might Jyoti Dadi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that her words helped instead of burdened, and proud that her story is shaping her granddaughter's choices 🙂

grounding: A young woman hears her grandmother's regret about not studying and treats it as a warning, choosing which risks now are worth her future peace.

Sunday. Ankita, twenty, was oiling Kamla Nani's hair on the balcony when Nani said quietly, "My sister and I stopped speaking in 1987 over a gold chain. I always meant to say sorry first. Then she died. I wish I had opened my mouth." Ankita's hands stopped. The words sat on her chest all evening like a stone.
Thursday. In the hostel Ankita reread a draft she had kept for a month: an email to Professor Rao asking to join his river-survey project. She had been too shy to send it. She thought of Nani's voice. Not a weight, she decided. A warning. Which silence would bother her at seventy?
Two weeks later. She had sent it and got an interview. That evening she phoned Nani. "You made me brave." Nani laughed. "Good. Someone should use my mistakes."

qa.q: What did Nani and her sister stop speaking over?
qa.a: They stopped speaking over a gold chain.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel on Sunday after Nani's words, and how had that changed by Thursday?
qa.a: At first she felt weighed down, as if the words sat on her chest like a stone; by Thursday she felt braver, taking them as a warning, not a weight.

qa.q: What choice did Ankita make at the turning point on Thursday?
qa.a: She asked herself which silence would bother her at seventy, and decided to send the email to Professor Rao she had been too shy to send.

qa.q: How might Nani feel hearing 'You made me brave'?
qa.a: She may feel some peace, since her regret has helped Ankita, which is why she laughs and says someone should use her mistakes.

Dear Ira,
Remember I said Nani was coming for Lohri? She stayed up with me after everyone slept, rubbing her knees by the heater, and told me something I can't shake. She topped her village school, but when her brothers went to college she was kept home. "I wish I'd argued," she said. "I wish I'd just asked once." She wasn't crying. She said it like a weather report.
For a day it felt heavy, like now I have to succeed for both of us. But I don't think she meant it that way. She squeezed my hand and said, "Don't carry mine. Just don't make your own."
So I'm doing the scary thing: I'm applying for the exchange semester, even though Papa thinks it's too far. If I don't get it, fine. At least I asked once.
Write soon,
Gurpreet

Onam, late night.
Nani was stringing the pookalam flowers with me this morning when she said, out of nowhere, "I came first in my class, you know. Then I was married at seventeen and never once asked for college. I wish I had said something, just once."
She said it softly, still sorting marigolds.

But tonight I don't think she meant it as a debt. More like a map with one road marked "I wish".
So what's worth the risk for me? Asking Professor Disha about the research internship, even if she says no. Telling Amma I want the hostel next year.
Future Pallavi, I hope you thank me.
